abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a foundational reconceptualization of procedural noise functions through the lens of spectral analysis and Fourier transform theory. Traditional approaches to noise generation in computer graphics rely on heuristic constructions that lack formal guarantees on their spectral properties. We introduce the Spectral Noise Manifold framework, which establishes a rigorous mathematical characterization of noise functions as distributions over compact manifolds in frequency space. This theoretical foundation enables a systematic approach to designing noise functions with arbitrary spectral envelopes, something previously achieved only through empirical parameter tuning. Our framework establishes connections between established methods such as Perlin noise and Simplex noise, revealing them as special cases within a broader class of manifold-constrained spectral distributions. We demonstrate that the proposed theory enables the construction of novel noise variants with anisotropic characteristics and controlled high-frequency behavior, addressing longstanding limitations in shape modeling applications. The mathematical apparatus developed here provides graphics practitioners with principled tools for noise synthesis, moving beyond the black-box parameter adjustment that has characterized the field. Experimental validation confirms that noise functions derived from our framework exhibit superior statistical properties and aesthetic qualities compared to conventional approaches, establishing a new paradigm for procedural content generation.

We present a theoretical analysis and algorithmic improvement to the widely-adopted gradient noise methods used in geometric modeling and surface synthesis. Existing approaches to computing analytical gradients for procedural noise functions suffer from discontinuities and directional biases that manifest as visual artifacts in rendering applications. Through rigorous mathematical analysis of the gradient field topology, we identify the fundamental source of these deficiencies in the current theoretical framework and derive corrected formulations that guarantee C1 continuity everywhere in the domain. Our analysis reveals that the anisotropy observed in standard implementations arises from systematic errors in the interpolation kernel derivatives, which we mathematically characterize and compensate for through a novel correction term. The proposed refinement maintains the computational efficiency of existing methods while eliminating the directional artifacts that plague interactive graphics applications. We provide closed-form expressions for the corrected gradients that can be directly substituted into existing rendering pipelines. Applications to displacement mapping, normal mapping, and physically-based rendering demonstrate significant visual improvements, particularly in animated scenes where temporal coherence artifacts were previously problematic. This work provides the graphics community with a theoretically justified and practically implementable solution to a long-standing problem in procedural texturing.

This paper introduces HoloRender, a novel real-time rendering system architected around the principles of differentiable rendering for holographic displays. Unlike conventional rendering pipelines designed for planar displays, HoloRender computes light transport in a unified framework that simultaneously optimizes both the visual content and the holographic wavefront required for light field reconstruction. The system employs a differentiable wave optics simulation at its core, enabling end-to-end optimization of scene parameters directly from rendered imagery through gradient descent. We present a novel light field representation that decomposes the complex wavefront into hierarchical angular basis functions, dramatically reducing computational complexity while maintaining visual fidelity for virtual reality applications. The architecture incorporates specialized GPU kernels for accelerated diffraction calculations, achieving interactive frame rates for scenes containing millions of procedural elements. Unlike previous approaches that treat display hardware as a post-processing step, our system co-designs scene geometry, materials, and lighting with the holographic constraints directly integrated into the rendering equation. Experimental results demonstrate that HoloRender produces autostereoscopic imagery with unprecedented depth cues and reduced visual fatigue compared to existing VR systems. This work establishes a new paradigm for display-aware rendering that fundamentally redefines the relationship between graphics pipeline design and output hardware.

We present an enhanced user interface system for interactive 3D shape modeling that significantly improves workflow efficiency through a novel input abstraction layer. Traditional shape modeling tools force users to work directly with low-level geometric representations, creating a substantial cognitive burden that impedes creative exploration in animation and visual computing applications. Our system introduces a semantic abstraction layer that mediates between user intent expressed through natural gestures and the underlying geometric operations, automatically selecting appropriate modeling primitives and suggesting procedurally relevant transformations. The architecture combines machine learning-based intent recognition with a constraint propagation engine that maintains geometric validity throughout the editing session. We implemented this interface within an established animation production pipeline, conducting user studies with professional animators that demonstrate a 47% reduction in modeling time for complex character geometry while maintaining precise artistic control. The system gracefully handles ambiguity in user input by presenting contextual options that align with current modeling context, drawing upon learned patterns from a curated dataset of professional workflows. This work provides the computer graphics community with a practically deployable solution that substantially augments human capabilities in shape modeling tasks without sacrificing the expressiveness that artists require.
